query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the thickness and continuity of the boride surface layer through an extended high‐temperature powder-pack boriding treatment will improve resistance to molten aluminum corrosion in boride‐based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components produced using conventional boriding parameters, having a standard boride layer.
generation.intervention: Implement an extended high-temperature powder-pack boriding treatment designed to increase the thickness and density of the surface boride layer.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum under typical hot-dip plating conditions (relevant temperatures and immersion times) where the boride layer remains structurally stable.
generation.structural_mediator: A thicker, more continuous, and dense boride layer that serves as an effective physical barrier.
generation.mechanism: A denser, thicker boride layer reduces the interdiffusion and direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying metal substrate, thereby minimizing corrosive attack through reduced aluminum ion penetration.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components treated with the extended boriding process will show lower rates of aluminum penetration and corrosion, evidenced by reduced corrosion depths and weight loss compared to components prepared by the conventional process.
generation.baseline: Performance and corrosion resistance of boride-based components with a standard boride layer produced under conventional powder-pack boriding conditions.
generation.boundary: The approach remains effective as long as the boride phase retains its integrity and does not undergo phase transformation or embrittlement under plating temperatures; beyond critical thickness or under extreme conditions, the benefits may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal treatment duration and temperature for achieving the protective layer without compromising mechanical integrity, as well as the critical layer thickness required for effective corrosion resistance, need further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical boride-based component samples. Subject one group to conventional boriding treatment and the other to the extended high-temperature powder-pack boriding intervention. Expose both groups to molten aluminum under controlled hot-dip plating conditions for a fixed duration. Post-exposure, analyze cross-sectional microstructure to measure boride layer thickness and quantify corrosion penetration.
measurements: Boride layer thickness (via SEM or optical microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the extended boriding treatment does not yield a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or greater corrosion depths, weight loss, or performance degradation compared to the conventionally treated samples).

## Abstract
AbstractThe CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys were treated by powder-pack boriding to improve their surface hardness and wear resistance. The variation of boriding layer thickness with time and temperature was studied. Then, the frequency factor D0 and diffusion activation energy Q of element B in HEA are calculated to be 9.15 × 10−5 m2/s and 206.93 kJ/mol, respectively. The diffusion behavior of elements in the boronizing process was investigated and shows that the boride layer forms with the metal atoms diffusing outward and the diffusion layer forms with the B atoms diffusing inward by the Pt-labeling method.
